title: Why does sizing ZGC in a container need more HEADROOM than G1 (ZGC is concurrent and needs room to allocate while it reclaims; colored pointers + page tables add native overhead) — why set `-Xmx` to only ~70–75% of the pod memory limit (reserving 25–30% for Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, Netty direct buffers, OS page cache) — and why does sizing the heap at ~90% of the limit get the pod `OOMKilled` by cgroups during a GC cycle?
shortTitle: Why sizing ZGC in a container needs more headroom than G1 — and why -Xmx at ~70-75% of the pod limit, not ~90%

s1_definition.profdef: In a container, the JVM's maximum heap is only part of its total memory footprint; Metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks, direct and mapped buffers, GC internal structures, and OS page cache all add to it. ZGC needs more headroom than G1 because it is fully concurrent and must keep allocating while it reclaims, and because colored pointers and extra page-table and memory-mapping machinery add native overhead. Setting `-Xmx` to only about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod memory limit reserves the rest for non-heap memory; setting it near ninety percent leaves too little, so during a GC cycle the total RSS exceeds the cgroup limit and the kernel OOM-kills the pod.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank rents a floor with a strict fire-safety occupancy limit (the pod memory limit). The main hall is the heap, but you also need corridors, stairwells, a staff room, and emptying space for the cleaning crew to shuffle furniture around (ZGC's concurrent work). If you cram the main hall to ninety percent of the floor's limit, there is no room for the crew to move desks during a clean-up, total occupancy crosses the fire limit, and the fire marshal (the cgroup OOM killer) evacuates the whole floor — the pod is killed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Heap is not the whole footprint; ZGC needs extra concurrent and native headroom, so set -Xmx to about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod limit, because ninety percent gets you OOM-killed mid-GC.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a container, the JVM's maximum heap is only part of its total memory footprint; Metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks, direct and mapped buffers, GC internal structures, and OS page cache all add to it. ZGC needs more headroom than G1 because it is fully concurrent and must keep allocating while it reclaims, and because colored pointers and extra page-table and memory-mapping machinery add native overhead. Setting `-Xmx` to only about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod memory limit reserves the rest for non-heap memory; setting it near ninety percent leaves too little, so during a GC cycle the total RSS exceeds the cgroup limit and the kernel OOM-kills the pod.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank rents a floor with a strict fire-safety occupancy limit (the pod memory limit). The main hall is the heap, but you also need corridors, stairwells, a staff room, and emptying space for the cleaning crew to shuffle furniture around (ZGC's concurrent work). If you cram the main hall to ninety percent of the floor's limit, there is no room for the crew to move desks during a clean-up, total occupancy crosses the fire limit, and the fire marshal (the cgroup OOM killer) evacuates the whole floor — the pod is killed.

**One line to remember:** Heap is not the whole footprint; ZGC needs extra concurrent and native headroom, so set -Xmx to about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod limit, because ninety percent gets you OOM-killed mid-GC.

sections.s2_technical:
A container has a hard memory limit enforced by the Linux cgroup. If the process's resident set size crosses that limit, the kernel OOM-killer terminates the process immediately, and Kubernetes records the pod as OOMKilled. Critically, the limit applies to total memory, not just the Java heap.

The JVM footprint is heap plus a lot of non-heap memory. Metaspace holds class metadata and grows with the number of loaded classes. The code cache holds JIT-compiled machine code. Each thread has a stack, typically around a megabyte, so hundreds of threads add hundreds of megabytes. Frameworks like Netty allocate direct byte buffers outside the heap for zero-copy I/O. There is GC-internal bookkeeping, thread-local allocation buffers, and the OS page cache for memory-mapped files. All of this lives inside the same cgroup limit as the heap.

ZGC needs more headroom than G1 for two reasons. First, it is fully concurrent: it reclaims while the application keeps allocating, so it must have free memory available to satisfy ongoing allocation during a collection — if the heap is sized right up to the limit, there is no slack to allocate into while relocation runs, and the collector cannot keep up. Second, ZGC's mechanics add native overhead: colored pointers rely on multi-mapping virtual memory, and the page tables and memory-mapping structures ZGC maintains consume native memory that G1 does not. So for the same heap, a ZGC process has a larger total footprint and needs more breathing room.

This is why the rule of thumb is to set `-Xmx` to about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod memory limit for ZGC, reserving the remaining twenty-five to thirty percent for everything non-heap. If instead you set the heap to about ninety percent of the limit, the non-heap memory plus the concurrent-allocation slack ZGC needs pushes total RSS over the cgroup limit, and it typically happens during a GC cycle precisely because that is when ZGC is allocating into fresh pages while relocating — so the pod gets OOMKilled at the worst moment, under load, during collection.

In modern JVMs you do not usually hardcode `-Xmx` in containers; you use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, which the JVM applies to the detected container limit. Setting `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70` to `75` for ZGC achieves the right headroom and survives changes to the pod limit. You should also set `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` so a true heap OOM fails fast and restarts cleanly rather than limping, and `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` with a fixed heap for latency-sensitive services. You verify headroom with Native Memory Tracking (`-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` read via `jcmd VM.native_memory`).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India moved its transfer API to Kubernetes with a two-gigabyte pod limit and, copying an old bare-metal setting, set the heap to roughly ninety percent of that. Under load the pods were randomly OOMKilled. This is the classic container heap-sizing mistake — the heap left no room for non-heap memory.

Problem 2 — The team had also switched to ZGC for latency, which needs even more headroom than the G1 they came from, so the kills got worse. This is the ZGC-needs-more-headroom problem — concurrent allocation slack plus colored-pointer native overhead.

Our mini-project is a runnable footprint reporter and sizing calculator: it reads the detected max heap, estimates the non-heap components, computes the recommended MaxRAMPercentage for ZGC versus G1 given a pod limit, and warns if the configured heap is too close to the limit. Classes are `ContainerSizingAdvisor` (driver and recommender), `FootprintReporter` (reads heap and non-heap beans), and `SizingPolicy` (encodes the percentage rules per collector).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
zgc-container-sizing/
├── pom.xml
├── Dockerfile
├── k8s/deployment.yaml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/container/
            ├── ContainerSizingAdvisor.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── FootprintReporter.java
```

Configuration (Kubernetes manifest + JVM flags):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml — pod memory limit must match JVM sizing
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer-api
          image: nbi/transfer-api:1.0.0
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "2Gi"      # request == limit for predictable sizing
            limits:
              memory: "2Gi"      # cgroup hard limit; OOMKill if RSS exceeds
          env:
            - name: JAVA_OPTS
              # ZGC headroom: heap ~72% of 2Gi, rest for non-heap
              value: >-
                -XX:+UseZGC
                -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=72.0
                -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
                -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
                -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
                -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,tags
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run inside a 2Gi memory limit to see container-aware sizing
docker run --rm --memory=2g nbi/transfer-api:1.0.0 \
  java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=72.0 -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
       -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary \
       -cp /app/zgc-container-sizing-1.0.0.jar \
       com.bank.jvm.container.ContainerSizingAdvisor

# Inspect the ACTUAL native footprint to verify headroom
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a pod memory limit of two thousand forty-eight megabytes, and two sizing policies — ZGC at seventy-two percent and G1 at eighty percent.

Step 1. `FootprintReporter` reads the heap max and the non-heap used from the memory beans, plus the thread count, and logs that non-heap memory — Metaspace, code cache, stacks, direct buffers — all counts against the same pod limit as the heap.

Step 2. The advisor computes the ZGC recommendation: seventy-two percent of two thousand forty-eight is about one thousand four hundred seventy-four megabytes for the heap, leaving roughly five hundred seventy-four megabytes for everything non-heap and for ZGC's concurrent-allocation slack.

Step 3. It computes the G1 recommendation at eighty percent, about one thousand six hundred thirty-eight megabytes, because G1 needs less headroom than ZGC — it does not carry the colored-pointer native overhead and does less concurrent allocation during collection.

Step 4. It then evaluates the dangerous ninety-percent setting, about one thousand eight hundred forty-three megabytes. `isTooClose` finds the remaining non-heap budget is under twenty percent, so it logs a severe warning that the cgroup will OOM-kill the pod during a GC cycle.

Step 5. The reason it happens during a GC cycle is that ZGC allocates into fresh pages while concurrently relocating, so total RSS peaks mid-collection; if the heap is already near the limit, that peak crosses it and the kernel kills the process.

Step 6. The logs give the operator concrete numbers: use about one thousand four hundred seventy-four megabytes of heap for ZGC on this pod, never one thousand eight hundred forty-three, and verify with Native Memory Tracking.

```

Oct 25, 2026 1:45:10 AM com.bank.jvm.container.FootprintReporter report
INFO: Remember: Metaspace + code cache + stacks + direct buffers + page cache ALL count against the pod limit

INFO: G1 recommended -Xmx ~ 1638MB (80.0%)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a container the thing that gets you killed is that the cgroup memory limit applies to the whole process footprint, not just the Java heap. The JVM's total memory is the heap plus a large amount of non-heap memory: Metaspace for class metadata, the code cache for JIT output, a roughly one-megabyte stack per thread, direct byte buffers that frameworks like Netty allocate off-heap for I/O, GC bookkeeping, and the operating-system page cache. All of that shares the same limit as the heap, and if the resident set size crosses the limit the kernel OOM-kills the process and Kubernetes marks the pod OOMKilled.

ZGC needs more headroom than G1 for two concrete reasons. It is fully concurrent, so it keeps reclaiming while the application keeps allocating, which means it must always have free memory to allocate into during a collection; if the heap is sized right up to the limit there is no slack and the collector cannot keep pace. And ZGC's colored pointers rely on multi-mapped virtual memory with extra page-table and mapping structures that consume native memory G1 does not use. So for the same heap, ZGC has a larger total footprint.

That is why I set the maximum heap to only about seventy to seventy-five percent of the pod limit for ZGC, reserving the remaining twenty-five to thirty percent for everything non-heap and for ZGC's concurrent-allocation slack, and in modern JVMs I express that as MaxRAMPercentage so it tracks the detected container limit rather than a hardcoded number. If instead you size the heap at around ninety percent, there is no room left, and the kill almost always happens during a GC cycle because that is exactly when ZGC is allocating into fresh pages while relocating, so the resident set peaks and crosses the limit under load. At National Bank of India our transfer API pods were being OOMKilled because someone had carried over a ninety-percent heap from bare metal; I moved them to MaxRAMPercentage of seventy-two with ExitOnOutOfMemoryError and AlwaysPreTouch, verified the real footprint with Native Memory Tracking, and the kills stopped.
